title: النقاش الأكادادمي / Academic seminar discussion
bridge: In Spanish, to express nuanced opinions in a seminar, you use structures like 'desde mi punto de vista' or 'si bien es cierto que...', supported by the subjunctive or conditional mood. In Arabic, academic courtesy is built with fixed formulas such as 'من وجهة نظري' and the conditional particle 'إنْ' (in) to qualify statements, but there is no equivalent subjunctive: modulation is achieved through modal particles (قَدْ، لعلّ) and the choice of perfective/imperfective aspect. A common mistake is to translate Spanish tenses literally, when Arabic prefers the modal imperfect (المضارع) for hypotheses and suggestions, not the perfective as in factual conditionals.
rule: For an academic discussion in Arabic (C1), you need to master the expression of opinion, nuanced agreement/disagreement, and reformulation. Use the الإضافة (idafa) construction for academic terms (مؤتمر البحث). To express an opinion: 'من وجهة نظري' (min wijhat naẓarī) + verb in the imperfect (يَرَى). For hypotheses: 'إنْ' (in) indicates a possible condition, and 'لو' (law) for unreal conditions; the imperfect is used for potential (يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَكُونَ) and 'قَدْ' for possibility (قَدْ يَكُونُ). For reformulation: 'بمعنى آخر' (bi-maʿnā ākhar). Agreement is expressed with 'أُوَافِقُكَ الرَّأْيَ' (uwāfiquka al-raʾy), and soft disagreement with 'وَلٰكِنْ مِنْ نَاحِيَةٍ أُخْرَى' (walākin min nāḥiya ukhrā). Avoid overusing 'لٰكِنْ' (but) for contrast; use 'بَيْنَمَا' (while) for parallel contrasts. Academic register requires phrases like 'مِنَ الجَدِيرِ بِالذِّكْرِ' (it is worth mentioning) and 'وِفْقًا لِلدِّرَاسَاتِ' (according to studies). Verbs of opinion are not conjugated in the simple conditional (there is no 'diría'), but are nuanced with 'قَدْ' or 'يُمْكِنُ'.

concept_examples.text: مِنْ وِجْهَةِ نَظَرِي، يُعَدُّ هَذَا الاِقْتِرَاحُ غَيْرَ وَافٍ بِالشُّرُوطِ المَطْلُوبَةِ.
concept_examples.translation: From my point of view, this proposal does not meet the required standards.
concept_examples.phonetic: /min wid͡ʒhat naðˤarī juʿaddu haːða‿l-iqtirāḥ ġayr wāfin bi-ʃʃurūṭ al-maṭlūba/

concept_examples.text: إِنْ كَانَ لِي أَنْ أُبْدِيَ مُلَاحَظَةً، فَإِنَّ النَّتائِجَ تَحْتَاجُ إِلَى تَدْعِيمٍ إِضَافِيٍّ.
concept_examples.translation: If I may make an observation, the results require additional support.
concept_examples.phonetic: /in kaːna lī ʾan ʾubdiya mulāḥaẓatan fa-ʾinna‿n-natāʾiǧ taḥtaːǧu ʾilā tadʿīmin ʾiḍāfiyy/

concept_examples.text: بَيْنَمَا يُشِيرُ البَاحِثُونَ إِلَى تَقَدُّمٍ مَلْمُوسٍ، تَبْقَى الفَجْوَةُ بَيْنَ النَّظَرِيَّةِ وَالتَّطْبِيقِ.
concept_examples.translation: While researchers point to notable progress, a gap remains between theory and practice.
concept_examples.phonetic: /bajnamaː juʃīru‿l-bāḥiṯūna ʾilā taqaddumin malmūsin tabqā‿l-faǧwaːtu bajna‿n-naẓariyya wa‿t-taṭbīq/

concept_examples.text: يُمكِنُنَا أَنْ نَسْتَنِدَ إلَى هَذِهِ المَعْطَيَاتِ لِدَعْمِ فَرَضِيَّتِنَا.
concept_examples.translation: We can rely on this data to support our hypothesis.
concept_examples.phonetic: /jumkinunā ʾan nastanida ʾilā haːdihi‿l-maʿṭayāt li-daʿmi faraḍiyyatinā/

common_error.wrong: أَنَا وَافَقُ مَعَ رَأْيِكَ، لٰكِنْ عِنْدِي مُلَاحَظَةٌ صَغِيرَة.
common_error.correct: أُوَافِقُكَ الرَّأْيَ، وَمَعَ ذٰلِكَ لَدَيَّ مُلَاحَظَةٌ بَسِيطَةٌ.
common_error.correct_alt: أَنَا مُوَافِقٌ لَكَ، لٰكِنْ مِنْ نَاحِيَةٍ أُخْرَى أَرَى أَنَّهُ يَنْقُصُنَا بَعْضُ التَّفَاصِيلِ.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs when translating 'I agree with you' literally as 'أَنَا وَافَقُ مَعَ رَأْيِكَ' instead of using the idiomatic construction 'أُوَافِقُكَ الرَّأْيَ' (verb + direct object 'you' + 'the opinion'). Additionally, the verb in Arabic is conjugated in the present tense, not the past, to express current action. The particle 'لٰكِنْ' is correct but stronger than 'and yet' (وَمَعَ ذٰلِكَ), which is more nuanced and academic. For a C1 register, avoid 'صَغِيرَة' (small) and prefer 'بَسِيطَة' (simple, minor).

examples.original: أَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ هَذِهِ المُعَالَجَةَ غَيْرُ دَقِيقَةٍ لِأَنَّهَا تَتَجَاهَلُ العَوَامِلَ السِّيَاقِيَّةَ.
examples.phonetic: /ʾaʿtaqidu ʾanna haːdihi‿l-muʿālaja ġayru daqīqatin li-ʾannahā tatajāhal al-ʿawāmil as-siyāqiyya/
examples.translation: I believe this approach is not precise because it ignores contextual factors.
examples.note: Use 'أَعْتَقِدُ' (I believe) for personal opinion, followed by 'أَنَّ' (that) and a nominal sentence.

examples.original: مِنْ وِجْهَةِ نَظَرِي، يَحْمِلُ هَذَا المَوْقِفُ تَنَاقُضًا بَيْنَ النَّظَرِيَّةِ وَالتَّطْبِيقِ.
examples.phonetic: /min wid͡ʒhat naðˤarī jaḥmilu haːða‿l-mawqif tanāquḍan bajna‿n-naẓariyya wa‿t-taṭbīq/
examples.translation: From my point of view, this stance contains a contradiction between theory and practice.
examples.note: The expression 'مِنْ وِجْهَةِ نَظَرِي' is more formal than 'أَعْتَقِدُ' and suitable for seminars.

examples.original: لَعَلَّ هَذِهِ النَّتِيجَةَ تُفْسِرُ بَعْضَ التَّنَاقُضَاتِ المَوْجُودَةِ فِي النَّصِّ.
examples.phonetic: /laʿalla haːdihi‿n-natīja tufassiru baʿḍa‿t-tanāquḍāt al-mawǧūda fī‿n-naṣṣ/
examples.translation: Perhaps this result explains some of the contradictions present in the text.
examples.note: The particle 'لَعَلَّ' (perhaps) introduces a hypothesis with a present verb. It is a subtle way to express possibility without commitment.

examples.original: أُوَافِقُكَ الرَّأْيَ فِي هَذِهِ النُّقْطَةِ، وَأَضِيفُ أَنَّ البَيَانَاتِ تُؤَيِّدُ هٰذَا الطَّرْحَ.
examples.phonetic: /ʾuwāfiquka‿r-raʾya fī haːdihi‿n-nuqṭa wa-ʾaḍīfu ʾanna‿l-bayānāt tuʾayyidu haːða‿ṭ-ṭarḥ/
examples.translation: I agree with you on this point, and I add that the data supports this proposal.
examples.note: Structure 'أُوَافِقُكَ الرَّأْيَ' + 'فِي' + topic. Add 'وَأَضِيفُ' to build upon the opinion.

examples.original: أَقْتَصِرُ عَلَى مُلَاحَظَةٍ مُتَوَاضِعَةٍ: هٰذَا التَّفْسِيرُ لَا يَأْخُذُ فِي الحُسْبَانِ الجَانِبَ الثَّقَافِيَّ.
examples.phonetic: /ʾaqtaṣiru ʿalā mulāḥaẓatin mutawāḍiʿa haːða‿t-tafsīr lā ʾaxuḏu fī‿l-ḥusbān al-ǧānib aṯ-ṯaqāfiyy/
examples.translation: I will limit myself to a humble observation: this interpretation does not take cultural aspects into account.
examples.note: Use 'أَقْتَصِرُ عَلَى' to introduce a gentle critique, avoiding confrontation.

examples.original: قَدْ يُوَافِقُكَ بَعْضُ الزُّمَلَاءِ، لٰكِنَّنِي لَسْتُ مُقْتَنِعًا بِالفَرَضِيَّةِ الأَصْلِيَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: /qad juwāfiquka baʿḍu‿z-zumalāʾ walākinnanī lastu muqtaniʿan bi‿l-faraḍiyya al-ʾaṣliyya/
examples.translation: Some colleagues may agree with you, but I am not convinced by the original hypothesis.
examples.note: The particle 'قَدْ' softens the verb, and 'لٰكِنَّنِي' introduces the objection. This is an indirect and diplomatic disagreement.

examples.original: لَوْ سَمَحْتُمْ، أَوَدُّ أَنْ أَعُودَ إِلَى نُقْطَةِ البَاحِثِ الأَوَّلِ لِتَوْضِيحِ فِكْرَتِي.
examples.phonetic: /law samaḥtum ʾawaddu ʾan ʾaʿūda ʾilā nuqṭati‿l-bāḥiṯ al-ʾawwal li-tawḍīḥ fikratī/
examples.translation: If you permit, I would like to return to the first researcher’s point to clarify my idea.
examples.note: The construction 'لَوْ سَمَحْتُمْ' + 'أَوَدُّ' (I would like) is a polite formula. Use it to take the floor.

examples.original: بِمَعْنَى آخَرَ، هٰذِهِ النَّتِيجَةُ تُشِيرُ إِلَى حَاجَةٍ مُلِحَّةٍ لِإِعَادَةِ النَّظَرِ فِي المَنْهَجِيَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: /bi-maʿnā ʾākhar haːdihi‿n-natīja tuʃīru ʾilā ḥāǧatin mulḥḥatan li-ʾiʿādati‿n-naẓar fī‿l-manhaǧiyya/
examples.translation: In other words, this result indicates an urgent need to re-examine the methodology.
examples.note: 'بِمَعْنَى آخَرَ' is perfect for reformulating an idea more clearly.

examples.original: وَإِذَا مَا أَخَذْنَا بِعَيْنِ الاِعْتِبَارِ المُتَغَيِّرَ الإِقْلِيمِيَّ، فَقَدْ نَصِلُ إِلَى اسْتِنْتَاجَاتٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ.
examples.phonetic: /wa-ʾiḏā mā ʾaxaḏnā biʿayni‿l-iʿtibār al-mutaġayyir al-ʾiqlīmiyya fa-qad naṣilu ʾilā stintāǧāt muḵtalifa/
examples.translation: And if we take the regional variable into account, we may arrive at different conclusions.
examples.note: The structure 'وَإِذَا مَا' + perfective + 'فَقَدْ' + imperfective expresses a potential condition with a probable result, typical of academic register.

title: التواصل المهني الرفيع المستوى / Professional high-level communication
bridge: In Spanish, professional courtesy often relies on the use of the conditional and phrases like 'podría' or 'sería posible'. In Arabic, this function is performed through the use of modal particles such as 'حتى' (ḥattā) to express purpose, 'لو' (law) for hypothetical conditions, and extensive use of the subjunctive in polite constructions. A typical error for Spanish speakers is to literally translate the Spanish conditional into Arabic, creating unnatural structures. Additionally, Arabic distinguishes between masculine and feminine in the verb, which in Spanish is only marked in some tenses, requiring special attention in formal contexts.
rule: In Modern Standard Arabic, high-level professional communication is characterized by: (1) addressing the recipient with the appropriate treatment (سيد/سيدة), (2) using verbs in the past or present with modal particles to soften requests, such as 'أرجو أن' (ʾarjū ʾan) and 'هل يمكن' (hal yumkin), (3) constructing hypotheses with 'لو' (law) + past + 'لـ' (la-) in the apodosis, and (4) using formal expressions of gratitude and closing. Note that the particle 'أن' (ʾan) introduces the subjunctive in Arabic, equivalent to the use of the subjunctive in Spanish after verbs of influence or desire, but in Arabic the verb is conjugated in the subjunctive mood (with the -a ending) and the simple conditional is not used. To express future actions or intentions in negotiation contexts, the construction 'سوف' (sawfa) or the present with future meaning is used. Gender agreement in verbs and adjectives is crucial, as in Arabic the verb agrees with the subject's gender in all persons, whereas in Spanish this only occurs in the third person. In formal meetings, the phrase 'حسب ما تم الاتفاق عليه' (ḥasab mā tamma al-ittifāq ʿalayhi) is used to refer to prior agreements. Dialectalisms should be avoided in formal written contexts.

concept_examples.text: أرجو أن تتفضلوا بقبول هذا العرض النهائي.
concept_examples.translation: I kindly request that you accept this final offer.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʾarjū ʾan tatafaḍḍalū bi-qabūl hāḏā al-ʿarḍ al-nihāʾī.

concept_examples.text: لو كان لدينا متسع من الوقت، لناقشنا المسألة بالتفصيل.
concept_examples.translation: If we had more time, we would discuss the matter in detail.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kāna ladaynā mutassaʿ min al-waqt, lanāqashnā al-masʾala bil-tafṣīl.

concept_examples.text: هل يمكن أن نؤجل هذا الاجتماع إلى الأسبوع القادم؟
concept_examples.translation: Could we postpone this meeting until next week?
concept_examples.phonetic: hal yumkin ʾan nuʾajjil hāḏā al-ijtimāʿ ʾilā al-usbūʿ al-qādim?

concept_examples.text: نقدّر عالياً تعاونكم ونأمل في استمرار العلاقة المهنية.
concept_examples.translation: We highly appreciate your cooperation and hope for the continuation of our professional relationship.
concept_examples.phonetic: nuqaddir ʿāliyan taʿāwunakum wa-naʾmal fī istimrār al-ʿalāqa al-mihaniyya.

common_error.explanation: The error stems from a literal translation of the Spanish conditional 'nos gustaría' or 'podríamos' using the future structure 'سوف' (sawfa), which sounds too direct and impolite in Arabic. In formal Arabic, politeness is expressed with verbs like 'نرجو' (narjū) or 'نأمل' (naʾmal) in the present, followed by 'أن' + subjunctive. Additionally, the respectful form 'تتفضلوا' (tatafaḍḍalū) must be used to maintain a formal tone.

examples.original: هل يمكنك إرسال التقرير في أقرب وقت؟
examples.phonetic: hal yumkinuka ʾirsāl al-taqrīr fī ʾaqrab waqt?
examples.translation: Could you send the report as soon as possible?
examples.note: Use of 'هل يمكن' (hal yumkin) to soften the request, instead of a direct imperative.

examples.original: أودّ أن أطلب منكم توضيح هذه النقطة.
examples.phonetic: ʾūddu ʾan ʾaṭlub minkum tawḍīḥ hāḏihi al-nuqṭa.
examples.translation: I would like to ask you to clarify this point.
examples.note: The expression 'أودّ أن' (ʾūddu ʾan) is equivalent to 'I would like' in Spanish and is followed by the subjunctive.

examples.original: هل يمكن أن نناقش هذا الموضوع في جلسة خاصة؟
examples.phonetic: hal yumkin ʾan nunāqish hāḏā al-mawḍūʿ fī jalsa ḫāṣṣa?
examples.translation: Could we discuss this topic in a private session?
examples.note: The verb 'نناقش' (nunāqish) is in the subjunctive due to the particle 'أن' (ʾan).

examples.original: لو أنجزنا المشروع في الوقت المحدد، لكان العميل راضياً.
examples.phonetic: law ʾanjaznā al-mashrūʿ fī al-waqt al-muḥaddad, lakāna al-ʿamīl rāḍiyan.
examples.translation: If we had completed the project on time, the client would have been satisfied.
examples.note: The construction 'لو' + past + 'لـ' indicates unreality, similar to the compound conditional in Spanish.

examples.original: لو كانت الميزانية كافية، لوسّعنا فريق العمل.
examples.phonetic: law kānat al-mīzāniyya kāfiya, lawassaʿnā farīq al-ʿamal.
examples.translation: If the budget were sufficient, we would expand the work team.
examples.note: The past 'كانت' is used with a hypothetical sense, not temporal, in this structure.

examples.original: إن أنتم وافقتم على الشروط، سنبدأ التنفيذ فوراً.
examples.phonetic: ʾin ʾantum wāfaqtum ʿalā al-shurūṭ, sanabdaʾ al-tanfīdh fawran.
examples.translation: If you accept the terms, we will begin execution immediately.
examples.note: The particle 'إن' (ʾin) introduces a real condition, and the apodosis uses 'سـ' (sa-) for future.

examples.original: نؤكد لكم التزامنا الكامل ببنود العقد الموقّع.
examples.phonetic: nuʾakkid lakum iltizām-nā al-kāmil bi-bunūd al-ʿaqd al-muwaqqaʿ.
examples.translation: We confirm our full commitment to the clauses of the signed contract.
examples.note: The verb 'نؤكد' (nuʾakkid) emphasizes commitment, and the adjective 'الكامل' agrees with the noun.

examples.original: نرجو من حضرتكم تزويدنا بالوثائق اللازمة.
examples.phonetic: narjū min ḥaḍratikum tazwīd-nā bil-wathāʾiq al-lāzima.
examples.translation: We kindly request that you provide us with the necessary documents.
examples.note: The treatment 'حضرتكم' (ḥaḍratikum) is formal and respectful, equivalent to 'usted' in Spanish.

examples.original: سوف نعمل على حل هذه المسألة في أقرب فرصة ممكنة.
examples.phonetic: sawfa naʿmal ʿalā ḥall hāḏihi al-masʾala fī ʾaqrab furṣa mumkina.
examples.translation: We will work to resolve this matter as soon as possible.
examples.note: The use of 'سوف' (sawfa) plus present expresses future, but note it is more direct than previous polite forms.

title: التحليل الأدبي والثقافي / Literary and cultural analysis
bridge: In Spanish, when analyzing literature or culture, we often use the subjunctive after negative opinion verbs ('No creo que sea...') and evaluative expressions. In Arabic, modality is expressed with particles like 'qad' (قد) and the 'inna' (إِنَّ) construction that emphasizes certainty, as well as the accusative case with 'anna' (أَنَّ) after verbs of knowledge. A typical error is to translate 'es posible que' literally as 'mumkin anna' instead of 'mumkin an' followed by the subjunctive, since 'anna' requires a noun in the accusative case, not a conjugated verb. Additionally, subject ellipsis is more flexible in Arabic, but gender and number agreement in critical descriptions (especially with non-human plurals) must treat the noun as feminine singular, which does not occur in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, to express literary and cultural analysis at C1 level, complex structures are used: 1) 'qad' (قد) + past indicates possibility or past certainty: 'qad kāna al-kitāb mu'aththiran' (قد كان الكتاب مؤثراً) – 'the book may have been influential' or 'it was surely influential' depending on context. 2) 'inna' (إِنَّ) and its sisters (anna, ka'anna, lakinna, layta, la'alla) modify the subject by putting it in the accusative: 'inna al-riwāyata tatajāwazu al-hudūd' (إِنَّ الرواية تتجاوز الحدود) – 'certainly the novel transcends boundaries'. 3) To express personal opinion, 'ra'yī' (رأيي) or 'min wijhat nazarī' (من وجهة نظري) is used followed by 'anna' + nominal clause, not verbal. 4) Non-human plurals (plurals of things or concepts) agree in feminine singular: 'al-mu'allafāt al-adabiyya tu'aththiru fī al-mujtama'' (المؤلفات الأدبية تؤثر في المجتمع) – 'literary works influence society' (the verb 'tu'aththiru' is in feminine singular). 5) For nuances of cultural nuance, idiomatic expressions like 'bayna al-sutūr' (بين السطور) – 'between the lines', or 'al-qirā'a al-naqdiyya' (القراءة النقدية) – 'critical reading' are used. 6) The use of 'lam' + imperfect (jazm) to negate the past: 'lam yasil al-kātib ilā al-ḥall' (لم يصل الكاتب إلى الحل) – 'the writer did not reach a solution'. Avoid direct translation of the Spanish subjunctive: in Arabic, doubt is expressed with 'rubba-mā' (رُبَّمَا) followed by present or past, or with 'laysa min al-mu'akkid' (ليس من المؤكد) + 'an' + subjunctive. The ellipsis of the copula verb 'to be' in the present is mandatory: one does not say 'al-riwāya hiya fā'iza' (الرواية هي فائزة) for 'the novel is a winner', but rather 'al-riwāya fā'iza' (الرواية فائزة), although 'hiya' can be added for emphasis, but then it functions as a separating pronoun.

concept_examples.text: يُحَلِّلُ النُّقَّادُ النَّصَّ مِنْ وِجْهَةِ نَظَرٍ ثَقَافِيَّةٍ
concept_examples.translation: Critics analyze the text from a cultural perspective.
concept_examples.phonetic: yuḥallilu al-nuqqādu al-naṣṣa min wijhati naẓarin thaqāfiyya

concept_examples.text: إِنَّ الرِّوَايَةَ تَعْكِسُ تَوَتُّرَاتٍ اِجْتِمَاعِيَّةً عَمِيقَةً
concept_examples.translation: Certainly, the novel reflects deep social tensions.
concept_examples.phonetic: inna al-riwāyata taʿkisu tawatturāt ijtimāʿiyya ʿamīqa

concept_examples.text: قَدْ يَكُونُ الْمَنْهَجُ الرِّوَائِيُّ مَوْضُوعَ جِدَالٍ بَيْنَ الدَّارِسِينَ
concept_examples.translation: The novelistic method may be the subject of debate among scholars.
concept_examples.phonetic: qad yakūnu al-manhaju al-riwāʾiyyu mawḍūʿa jidālin bayna al-dārisīn

concept_examples.text: لَا يَقْتَصِرُ الْأَدَبُ عَلَى التَّصْوِيرِ؛ بَلْ يُعِيدُ تَشْكِيلَ الْهَوِيَّةِ الثَّقَافِيَّةِ
concept_examples.translation: Literature is not limited to representation; rather, it reshapes cultural identity.
concept_examples.phonetic: lā yaqtaṣiru al-adabu ʿalā al-taṣwīr; bal yuʿīdu tashkīla al-huwiyya al-thaqāfiyya

common_error.wrong: أَنَّ الرِّوَايَةَ تُؤَكِّدُ عَلَى الْقِيمِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ
common_error.correct: إِنَّ الرِّوَايَةَ تُؤَكِّدُ عَلَى الْقِيمِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ
common_error.explanation: The most frequent error is using 'anna' (أَنَّ) at the beginning of an independent sentence to emphasize, when 'inna' (إِنَّ) should be used instead. 'Anna' is used after verbs like 'I know that' (أَعْلَمُ أَنَّ) or 'I think that' (أَظُنُّ أَنَّ), while 'inna' is the emphatic particle that heads nominal sentences. In Spanish, the distinction between 'que' (subordinating) and 'ciertamente' (emphatic adverb) is clear, but in Arabic the confusion leads to a grammatical error. Additionally, in the correct alternative sentence, the particle is omitted, which is possible and common in Arabic, but emphasis is lost. To avoid this, remember: if the sentence is independent and you want to give emphasis, use 'inna'; if it is subordinate, use 'anna'.

examples.original: تَتَنَاسَجُ الْخُطُوطُ السَّرْدِيَّةُ فِي هَذِهِ الرِّوَايَةِ بِإِتْقَانٍ بَدِيعٍ
examples.phonetic: tatanāsaju al-khuṭūṭu al-sardiyya fī hādhihi al-riwāya bi-itqānin badīʿ
examples.translation: The narrative lines in this novel interweave with exquisite skill.
examples.note: Use of the present verb for a general truth, and the adjective 'badīʿ' (بديع) to qualify the quality.

examples.original: يُوَظِّفُ الْكَاتِبُ الرَّمْزِيَّةَ لِإِبْرَازِ الصِّرَاعِ الدَّاخِلِيِّ
examples.phonetic: yuwaẓẓifu al-kātibu al-ramziyya li-ibrāz al-ṣirāʿ al-dākhilī
examples.translation: The writer employs symbolism to highlight the internal conflict.
examples.note: Verb 'yuwaẓẓif' (employs) with direct object; 'li-ibrāz' (to highlight) uses the preposition 'li' + masdar.

examples.original: تَتَعَذَّرُ قِرَاءَةُ الرِّوَايَةِ بِمَعْزِلٍ عَنْ السِّيَاقِ التَّارِيخِيِّ
examples.phonetic: tataʿadhdharu qirāʾatu al-riwāya bi-maʿzilin ʿan al-siyāq al-tārīkhī
examples.translation: Reading the novel proves impossible when divorced from its historical context.
examples.note: Structure 'tataʿadhdharu' (proves difficult) + masdar; use of 'bi-maʿzilin ʿan' (when divorced from).

examples.original: تَخْتَلِفُ الرُّؤْيَةُ الْعَالَمِيَّةُ بَيْنَ الْمَشْرِقِ وَالْمَغْرِبِ فِي تَنَاوُلِ الْمَرْأَةِ
examples.phonetic: takhtalifu al-ruʾyā al-ʿālamiyya bayna al-mashriq wa al-maghrib fī tanāwul al-marʾa
examples.translation: The worldview differs between the East and West in the portrayal of women.
examples.note: Use of 'takhtalif' (differs) with 'bayna...wa...' (between...and...); correct agreement in feminine singular.

examples.original: يُمْكِنُ أَنْ نُقَارِنَ بَيْنَ الرِّوَايَةِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالرِّوَايَةِ الْإِسْبَانِيَّةِ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْبُنْيَةِ
examples.phonetic: yumkinu an nuqārina bayna al-riwāya al-ʿarabiyya wa al-riwāya al-isbāniyya min ḥaythu al-bunya
examples.translation: We can compare the Arabic novel and the Spanish novel in terms of structure.
examples.note: Use of 'yumkinu an' (it is possible to) followed by subjunctive (nuqārina). This avoids the error of using 'anna'.

examples.original: تُظْهِرُ الْمُقَارَنَةُ أَوْجُهَ الشَّبَهِ وَالِاخْتِلَافِ فِي الْمُعَالَجَاتِ النَّقْدِيَّةِ
examples.phonetic: tuẓhiru al-muqārana awjuh al-shabah wa al-ikhtilāf fī al-muʿālajāt al-naqdiyya
examples.translation: The comparison reveals aspects of similarity and difference in critical approaches.
examples.note: Use of 'awjuh' (aspects), the plural of 'wajh' (face), and agreement with 'al-shabah' (similarity).

examples.original: يُجَادِلُ النَّاقِدُ بِأَنَّ النَّصَّ يُفَكِّكُ بِنْيَةَ السُّلْطَةِ
examples.phonetic: yujādilu al-nāqidu bi-anna al-naṣṣa yufakkiku binyat al-sulṭa
examples.translation: The critic argues that the text deconstructs the structure of power.
examples.note: Use of 'yujādilu bi-anna' (argues that) – here 'anna' is correct because it follows a verb of opinion.

examples.original: لَوْ لَمْ يَكُنِ الْأَدَبُ مُلْتَزِمًا، لَمَا نَاقَشَ الْقَضَايَا الْجَوْهَرِيَّةَ
examples.phonetic: law lam yakuni al-adabu multaziman, lamā nāqasha al-qaḍāyā al-jawhariyya
examples.translation: Had literature not been committed, it would not have addressed core issues.
examples.note: Conditional sentence with 'law' (if) + 'lam' (negation) + jazm; the apodosis with 'lamā' (then it would not).

examples.original: مِنْ الصَّعْبِ أَنْ نُحَدِّدَ مَدَى تَأْثِيرِ النَّصِّ فِي الْقَارِئِ
examples.phonetic: mina al-ṣaʿbi an nuḥaddida madā taʾthīr al-naṣṣi fī al-qāriʾ
examples.translation: It is difficult to determine the extent of the text's influence on the reader.
examples.note: Structure 'mina al-ṣaʿbi an' (it is difficult to) + subjunctive; 'madā' (extent).

examples.original: تَتَجَلَّى الْعَلَاقَةُ الْجَدَلِيَّةُ بَيْنَ النَّصِّ وَالْوَاقِعِ فِي الْمَبْنَى
examples.phonetic: tatajallā al-ʿalāqa al-jadaliyya bayna al-naṣṣi wa al-wāqiʿi fī al-mabnā
examples.translation: The dialectical relationship between the text and reality manifests in the structure.
examples.note: Use of 'tatajallā' (manifests) and 'al-mabnā' (structure) – a technical term.

title: التفكير الفلسفي والتجريد / Philosophical and abstract reasoning
bridge: In Spanish, to express hypotheses or unreal conditions we use the subjunctive and conditional moods. In Arabic, these nuances are conveyed through different syntactic structures, such as using 'لو' (law) for unreal conditions and 'كان' (kāna) with the present tense to express unreality. The absence of a subjunctive mood as such in Arabic means that Spanish speakers must learn to use particles and verb tenses differently to nuance probability, doubt, or counterfactuals. Additionally, Arabic uses 'idhā' for possible conditions and 'law' for impossible or hypothetical ones, a distinction that is not as clearly marked in Spanish.
rule:
To express abstract and philosophical reasoning in Arabic at a C1 level, the following structures are used:
1. **Unreal conditionals**: 'لو' (law) + verb in perfect past (māḍī), followed by 'لَ' (la) + verb in perfect past or present. Example: لو كان الإنسان حراً لما اختار الحروب (law kāna al-insānu ḥurran lamā ikhtāra al-ḥurūb).
2. **Possible conditionals**: 'إذا' (idhā) + present or past + response in present or future. Example: إذا فكر الإنسان بعمق أدرك حقيقة الوجود (idhā fakkara al-insānu bi-ʿumqin adraka ḥaqīqata al-wujūd).
3. **Expression of doubt or probability**: 'لعلّ' (laʿalla) is used with a noun or pronoun in the accusative, followed by the present tense. Example: لعل السعادة في القناعة (laʿalla al-saʿādata fī al-qanāʿa).
4. **Negation of reality**: 'ليس' (laysa) is used with nouns or 'ما' (mā) with verbs to negate essence or action, a nuance that in Spanish is expressed with 'no es' or 'no es que'.
5. **Philosophy of being**: the verb 'كان' (kāna) and its sisters (kāna wa akhawātuhā) invert the nominal order, giving a nuance of becoming or essential state, as in 'كان الإنسان واعياً' (kāna al-insānu wāʿiyan), meaning 'the man was conscious'.
6. **Use of masdar (verbal noun)**: to abstract actions, Arabic transforms verbs into abstract nouns (masdar). For example, 'sociedad' in Spanish is expressed through a masdar in Arabic. The preference for the masdar in philosophical Arabic is notable.
7. **Concordance rules**: when speaking of abstract concepts, the adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun, but in abstracts it is usually feminine singular (e.g., الحرية هي حق الإنسان - al-ḥurriyya hiya ḥaqqu al-insān).
8. **Exceptions**: in the expression of unreal conditions, if 'لو' is used with the present tense, 'كان' must be placed before the verb to maintain unreality (e.g., لو كان يفهم لما أخطأ).
9. **Accusative case**: after 'لعلّ' and similar particles, the noun must take the -a (fatha) ending to indicate the accusative, though in colloquial speech it is sometimes omitted.

concept_examples.text: الحرية ليست أن تفعل ما تشاء، بل أن تتحمل مسؤولية اختياراتك.
concept_examples.translation: Freedom is not doing what you want, but rather taking responsibility for your choices.
concept_examples.phonetic: al-ḥurriyya laysat an tafʿala mā tashāʾu bal an tataḥammala masʾūliyyata ikhtiyārātik.

concept_examples.text: لو كان العقل مقياساً للحقيقة لاختلفت الحقائق باختلاف العقول.
concept_examples.translation: If reason were a measure of truth, truths would differ according to minds.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kāna al-ʿaqlu miqyāsan lil-ḥaqīqati laʿkhtalafat al-ḥaqāʾiqu bi-ʿkhtilāfi al-ʿuqūl.

concept_examples.text: ما الوجود إلا سعي مستمر نحو معنى يتجاوز ذاته.
concept_examples.translation: Existence is nothing but a constant pursuit of meaning that transcends itself.
concept_examples.phonetic: mā al-wujūdu illā saʿyun mustamirrun naḥwa maʿnan yatajāwazu dhātahu.

concept_examples.text: لعل الحكمة أن تدرك حدود معرفتك قبل أن تدّعي امتلاكها.
concept_examples.translation: Perhaps wisdom is recognizing the limits of your knowledge before claiming to possess it.
concept_examples.phonetic: laʿalla al-ḥikmata an tudrika ḥudūda maʿrifatika qabla an taddaʿī imtilākahā.

common_error.explanation: The error arises because in Spanish an explicit pronoun ('if I were free') is used, and the speaker transfers this literally to Arabic. In Arabic, the verb ending already indicates the person, so the independent pronoun 'أنا' is unnecessary unless for emphasis. Additionally, when using 'لو', the past tense (كنت) must be used, not the present. The alternative with 'أنّي' is correct but more formal and emphatic.

examples.original: ليس كل ما يبدو بديهياً هو حقيقي بالضرورة.
examples.phonetic: laysa kullu mā yabdū badīhiyyan huwa ḥaqīqiyyun bil-ḍarūra.
examples.translation: Not everything that seems obvious is necessarily real.
examples.note: The negation particle 'ليس' (laysa) is used to deny essence, reinforcing the abstract nature of the statement.

examples.original: قد تكون الشكوكية أساساً للتحقق من صحة الأفكار.
examples.phonetic: qad takūnu al-shukūkiyya asāsan lil-taḥaqquqi min ṣiḥḥati al-afkār.
examples.translation: Skepticism can be a basis for verifying the validity of ideas.
examples.note: The particle 'قد' (qad) with the present tense expresses possibility; note that the verb 'تكون' is in the subjunctive (mansūb) after 'قد'.

examples.original: إنّ الوجود عند الفلاسفة الوجوديين هو ما يُدرك بالذات لا بالعقل فقط.
examples.phonetic: inna al-wujūda ʿinda al-falāsifati al-wujūdiyyīna huwa mā yudraku bil-ḏāti lā bil-ʿaqli faqaṭ.
examples.translation: According to existentialist philosophers, existence is what is perceived by the self, not just by reason.
examples.note: The particle 'إنّ' (inna) is used for emphasis, and the predicate is introduced with 'هو' (huwa) as a separator pronoun to clarify identity.

examples.original: كان الوجود يُفسَّر في القديم بأنه مادة وصورة.
examples.phonetic: kāna al-wujūdu yufassaru fī al-qadīmi bi-annahu māddatun wa ṣūra.
examples.translation: In ancient times, existence was explained as matter and form.
examples.note: The verb 'كان' introduces the past tense, and its sister 'أنّ' after the preposition 'بـ' (bi) turns the phrase into a nominal sentence.

examples.original: لو لم تكن الحرية مبنية على المسؤولية لأصبحت فوضى.
examples.phonetic: law lam takun al-ḥurriyya mabniyyatan ʿalā al-masʾūliyya laʾṣbaḥat fawḍā.
examples.translation: If freedom were not based on responsibility, it would become chaos.
examples.note: The use of 'لو لم' (law lam) to negate an unreal condition, followed by the response with 'لـ' (la). The verb 'أصبح' (aṣbaḥa) indicates transformation.

examples.original: إنّ الأخلاق ليست وصفات جاهزة، بل حوار دائم بين المبادئ والواقع.
examples.phonetic: inna al-ʾakhlāqa laysat waṣafāt jāhizatan, bal ḥiwārun dāʾimun bayna al-mabādiʾi wa-l-wāqiʿ.
examples.translation: Ethics is not ready-made recipes, but a constant dialogue between principles and reality.
examples.note: The negation 'ليست' (laysat) is used after a feminine noun; 'بل' (bal) introduces the correction.

examples.original: إذا اعتمد الإنسان على المنفعة وحدها في قراراته الأخلاقية، فقد يفقد البوصلة الداخلية.
examples.phonetic: idhā ʿtamada al-insānu ʿalā al-manfaʿati waḥdahā fī qarārātihi al-ʾakhlāqiyya, fa-qad yafqidu al-būṣṣala al-dākhiliyya.
examples.translation: If a person relies solely on utility in their ethical decisions, they may lose their internal compass.
examples.note: The particle 'إذا' (idhā) is used for possible conditions, and the result is preceded by 'فـ' (fa) followed by 'قد' to indicate possibility.

title: التعليق الاجتماعي-السياسي المتقدم / Advanced sociopolitical commentary
bridge: In Spanish, to express opinions about politics or society, we often use structures like 'es cierto que' (it's true that), 'hay que tener en cuenta que' (one must take into account that), or the subjunctive. In Arabic, advanced sociopolitical commentary is characterized by the frequent use of the maṣdar (المصدر) to nominalize actions, emphasis structures with 'inna' (إنَّ), and constructions of obligation with 'la budda' (لا بُدَّ) or 'min al-ḍarūrī' (من الضروري). A common error for Spanish speakers is to translate clauses with 'que' literally and forget that Arabic often prefers nominalization and VSO word order in formal contexts. Additionally, the particle 'qad' (قد) can nuance certainty, something without a direct equivalent in Spanish.
rule:
To produce advanced sociopolitical commentary in Arabic, a series of grammatical and rhetorical resources at C1 level are employed:

1. **Nominalization with maṣdar**: The use of the action noun (مصدر) is preferred to express abstract ideas, e.g., 'al-inḥirāf' (الانحراف) instead of 'that it deviates'. This is constructed with 'anna' (أنَّ) + subjunctive verb, or directly with the maṣdar as subject or complement.

2. **Sentences with 'inna' (إنَّ) for emphasis**: In formal registers, 'inna' is placed at the beginning to emphasize a statement. After 'inna', the subject takes the accusative case (e.g., 'inna l-ḥukūmata...'). In colloquial contexts, this is lost, but at C1 level, its correct use is expected.

3. **Expressions of obligation and necessity**: Structures like 'la budda' (لا بُدَّ) + genitive, 'min al-ḍarūrī' (من الضروري) + 'an' + subjunctive, or 'yajibu an' (يجب أن) + subjunctive are used. The choice depends on the degree of formality and nuance.

4. **Use of 'qad' (قد) for probability or certainty**: 'Qad' + perfective verb indicates that something has occurred (certainty), while 'qad' + imperfective verb indicates probability. This nuance has no exact parallel in Spanish and requires practice.

5. **Advanced discourse connectors**: To argue, structures like 'min nāḥiyatin ukhra' (من ناحية أخرى) 'on the other hand', 'bi-l-ḍarūrati' (بالضرورة) 'necessarily', 'fī ḥīna' (في حين) 'whereas', 'wa in kāna' (وإن كان) 'even if' are used.

6. **Passive voice and impersonal structures**: The passive is formed with 'fī' (في) or through verb conjugation in the passive form (e.g., 'yurā' يُرى 'it is seen'). Impersonal structures like 'min al-mu'akkad' (من المؤكد) 'it is certain that' are also common.

7. **Typical errors**: Spanish speakers tend to use 'hādhā huwa' (هذا هو) for 'this is', but in formal Arabic the pronoun 'huwa' can often be omitted if the context is clear. They also confuse 'lākin' (لكن) with 'wa lākin' (ولكن) when preceded by 'wa' at the start of a sentence.

concept_examples.text: إنَّ تدهور الأوضاع الاقتصادية يؤدي إلى زيادة الاحتقان الاجتماعي.
concept_examples.translation: The deterioration of economic conditions leads to increased social unrest.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʔinna tadahwur al-ʔawḍāʕ al-iqtiṣādiyya yuʔaddī ʔilā ziyādat al-iḥtiqān al-iǧtimāʕī.

concept_examples.text: لا بُدَّ من مراجعة السياسات العمومية لمواجهة تحديات العصر.
concept_examples.translation: It is essential to review public policies to address the challenges of the era.
concept_examples.phonetic: lā budda min murāǧaʕat al-siyāsāt al-ʕumūmiyya li-muwāǧahat taḥaddiyāt al-ʕaṣr.

concept_examples.text: قد تكون الإصلاحات بطيئة، لكنها ضرورية لتحقيق الاستقرار.
concept_examples.translation: Reforms may be slow, but they are necessary to achieve stability.
concept_examples.phonetic: qad takūn al-ʔiṣlāḥāt baṭīʔa, lākinna-hā ḍarūriyya li-taḥqīq al-istiqrār.

concept_examples.text: من ناحية أخرى، يرى بعض المحللين أن الحلول الجزئية غير كافية.
concept_examples.translation: On the other hand, some analysts believe that partial solutions are insufficient.
concept_examples.phonetic: min nāḥiyatin ʔuḵrā, yarā baʕḍ al-muḥallilīn ʔan al-ḥulūl al-ǧuzʔiyya ġayr kāfiya.

common_error.wrong: هذا هو الوضع خطير جدا في المنطقة.
common_error.correct: إنَّ الوضع خطيرٌ جداً في المنطقة.
common_error.explanation: The error lies in translating 'this is' literally as 'hādhā huwa' (هذا هو) and then omitting the verb 'es', but in Arabic, the emphatic structure with 'inna' (إنَّ) is more natural for expressing a categorical assertion. Additionally, using 'hādhā huwa' results in redundancy and a colloquial register. In formal Arabic, the construction with 'inna' at the beginning of the sentence is preferred, which places the subject in the accusative case (though this is not visible in unvocalized writing). Another correct alternative is the simple nominal sentence without 'inna', which is also correct but lacks emphasis.

examples.original: أرى أن السياسات الحالية لا تلبي طموحات الشباب.
examples.phonetic: ʔarā ʔan al-siyāsāt al-ḥāliyya lā tulabbī ṭumūḥāt al-šabāb.
examples.translation: I believe that current policies do not meet the aspirations of young people.
examples.note: Use of the verb 'رأى' (to see/opine) followed by 'أنَّ' + nominal clause. Note that 'أنَّ' requires the subject to be in the accusative case, though here it is feminine and not marked.

examples.original: من وجهة نظري، الإصلاح السياسي هو أولوية قصوى.
examples.phonetic: min waǧhat naẓarī, al-ʔiṣlāḥ al-siyāsī huwa ʔawlawiyya quṣwā.
examples.translation: From my point of view, political reform is a top priority.
examples.note: The expression 'من وجهة نظري' is equivalent to 'from my point of view'. The use of 'هو' is optional for emphasis but not necessary in a nominal sentence.

examples.original: يُعتقد أن المشاركة الشعبية ضرورية لنجاح أي مشروع إصلاحي.
examples.phonetic: yuʕtaqad ʔan al-mušāraka al-šaʕbiyya ḍarūriyya li-naǧāḥ ʔay mašrūʕ ʔiṣlāḥī.
examples.translation: It is believed that popular participation is essential for the success of any reform project.
examples.note: Use of the passive 'يُعتقد' (it is believed) to create an impersonal structure, common in formal commentary.

examples.original: رغم الإنجازات المحققة، لا تزال هناك فجوة كبيرة بين الخطاب والممارسة.
examples.phonetic: raġm al-ʔinǧāzāt al-muḥaqqiqa, lā tazāl hunāka fuǧwa kabīra bayn al-ḫiṭāb wa-l-mumārasa.
examples.translation: Despite the achievements made, there remains a significant gap between discourse and practice.
examples.note: The conjunction 'رغم' (despite) introduces a complement with a noun and the passive participle 'المحققة'. It is recommended to avoid using 'لكن' in the same sentence.

examples.original: في حين أن الحكومة تصر على نجاحها، يبدو أن المواطنين غير مقتنعين.
examples.phonetic: fī ḥīna ʔan al-ḥukūma tuṣirru ʕalā naǧāḥi-hā, yabdū ʔan al-muwāṭinīn ġayr muqtanʕīn.
examples.translation: While the government insists on its success, it seems that citizens are unconvinced.
examples.note: Use of 'في حين أن' (whereas) to contrast. In the second clause, 'يبدو أن' followed by 'أنَّ' and a nominal clause.

examples.original: يرجع السبب الأساسي لهذه الأزمة إلى سوء الإدارة.
examples.phonetic: yarǧiʕu al-sabab al-ʔasāsī li-hāḏihi al-ʔazma ʔilā sūʔ al-ʔidāra.
examples.translation: The root cause of this crisis can be traced back to poor management.
examples.note: The verb 'يرجع إلى' means 'to be traced back to, attributed to'. At advanced levels, it is frequently used to explain causes.

examples.original: بالمقارنة مع التجارب السابقة، يتضح أن الحلول الدبلوماسية أكثر فعالية.
examples.phonetic: bi-l-muqārana maʕa al-taǧārib al-sābiqa, yatawaḍḍaḥ ʔan al-ḥulūl al-diblūmāsiyya ʔakṯar faʕʕāliyya.
examples.translation: Compared to previous experiences, it becomes clear that diplomatic solutions are more effective.
examples.note: Use of 'بالمقارنة مع' (compared to) and the impersonal verb 'يتضح' (it becomes clear) to introduce conclusions.

examples.original: لذا، يمكن القول إن المستقبل يعتمد على قدرة المجتمع المدني على تنظيم نفسه.
examples.phonetic: li-ḏālika, yumkin al-qawl ʔinna al-mustaqbal yaʕtamid ʕalā qudrat al-muǧtamaʕ al-madanī ʕalā tanẓīm nafsih.
examples.translation: Thus, it can be said that the future depends on the ability of civil society to organize itself.
examples.note: The phrase 'يمكن القول إن' (it can be said that) is an advanced expression for conclusions. Note the use of 'إن' after 'القول'.

examples.original: وإن كان البعض يعترض على هذا الطرح، فالواقع يؤكد صحته.
examples.phonetic: wa-ʔin kān al-baʕḍ yaʕtariḍ ʕalā hāḏā al-ṭarḥ, fa-l-wāqiʕ yuʔakkid ṣiḥḥatah.
examples.translation: Even if some object to this approach, reality confirms its validity.
examples.note: The construction 'وإن كان' (even if) followed by 'فـ' (then) at the start of the main clause is an advanced formal feature.

title: السرد الشخصي المعقد بمنظور مستقبلي / Complex Personal Narratives with Future Perspective
bridge: In Spanish, to narrate events with a future perspective from the past, you use the compound conditional (habría hecho) or the past future (iba a hacer). In Modern Standard Arabic, complex future perspectives from the past are expressed using modal verb structures with كَانَ (kāna) + particle + imperfect verb, or the use of سَوْفَ / سَـ (sa-/sawfa) within indirect speech. The main trap is that Arabic lacks a direct equivalent to the compound conditional; instead, it combines the particle كَانَ with the verb in the subjunctive mood (منصوب) or with قد (qad), and word order and gender/number agreement differ from Spanish. Another key point: in Arabic, temporal perspective is often conveyed through context and particles rather than verbal inflection, which can lead Spanish speakers to overuse the simple past form.
rule: In Modern Standard Arabic, to express a future action viewed from a past reference point (future in the past), use the structure: كَانَ (kāna) in the past + أَنْ (an) + imperfect verb (subjunctive) or directly an imperfect verb preceded by سَـ (sa-) or سَوْفَ (sawfa) within an established past context. For example: كَانَ يَقُولُ إِنَّهُ سَيَذْهَبُ (kāna yaqūlu innahu sayadhhabu) = 'He said he would go.' Also used is كَانَ + سَيَذْهَبُ (kāna sayadhhabu) = 'He would go/had to go' (future in the past without indirect speech). The particle كَانَ is conjugated in the past (كَانَ، كَانَتْ، كَانُوا...), and the main verb remains in the imperfect, respecting gender and number agreement. Another form is كَانَ سَوْفَ يَذْهَبُ (kāna sawfa yadhhabu) with a similar meaning, though less common. For complex narratives, the past perfect (كُنْتُ قَدْ فَعَلْتُ) is frequently used for actions prior to other past actions, and the future in the past for subsequent actions. Exceptions: in spoken Arabic (e.g., Egyptian or Levantine), كَانَ هَيِكْتُب (kān hayiktib) is used instead of the standard form; however, C1 level requires mastery of the standard. The verb كَانَ in the past can also be used with a noun or adjective to express past states, but this is not part of this concept. Spanish speakers should avoid translating 'habría' literally as a single word; in Arabic, it is broken down into two elements.

concept_examples.text: كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ سَيَأْتِي إِلَى الحَفْلَةِ.
concept_examples.translation: I thought he would come to the party.
concept_examples.phonetic: kuntu ʔaẓunnu ʔannahu sayəʔtī ʔilā l-ḥaflati.

concept_examples.text: قَالَتْ إِنَّهَا سَتَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً طَوِيلَةً.
concept_examples.translation: She said she would write a long letter.
concept_examples.phonetic: qālat ʔinnahā sataktubu risālatan ṭawīlatan.

concept_examples.text: كَانَ مِنَ المُتَوَقَّعِ أَنْ يَنْجَحَ فِي الامْتِحَانِ.
concept_examples.translation: It was expected that he would pass the exam.
concept_examples.phonetic: kāna mina l-mutawaqqaʕi ʔan yanjaḥa fī l-ʔimtiḥāni.

concept_examples.text: عِنْدَمَا كُنْتُ صَغِيرًا، كَانَ جَدِّي يَقُولُ لِي إِنَّ السَّفَرَ سَيُغَيِّرُ حَيَاتِي.
concept_examples.translation: When I was little, my grandfather used to tell me that traveling would change my life.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʕindamā kuntu ṣaɣīran, kāna jaddī yaqūlu lī ʔinna s-safara sayuɣayyiru ḥayātī.

common_error.wrong: كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ يَأْتِي إِلَى الحَفْلَةِ.
common_error.correct: كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ سَيَأْتِي إِلَى الحَفْلَةِ.
common_error.correct_alt: كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ سَوْفَ يَأْتِي إِلَى الحَفْلَةِ.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish, the simple conditional (vendría) is often translated mentally by Spanish speakers as a simple imperfect in Arabic. However, in Arabic, to mark future-in-the-past, it is mandatory to add the prefix سَـ (sa-) or the particle سَوْفَ (sawfa) before the imperfect verb; otherwise, the sentence is interpreted as present within the past context (he comes), losing the future perspective. To avoid this, remember that any future action from a past point must carry an explicit future marker.

levels.label: المستقبل في الماضي مع كَانَ
levels.translation: Future in the past with كَانَ (kāna)

examples.original: كَانَ سَيَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ.
examples.phonetic: kāna sayadhhabu ʔilā s-sūqi.
examples.translation: He was going to go to the market.
examples.note: Use of كَانَ (past) + سَـ (future) + imperfect verb to express a future intention from the past.

examples.original: كُنْتُ سَأُسَافِرُ لَوْ كَانَ لَدَيَّ المَالُ.
examples.phonetic: kuntu saʔusāfiru law kāna ladayya l-mālu.
examples.translation: I would have traveled if I had had the money.
examples.note: In this construction, كُنْتُ سَأُسَافِرُ expresses a past conditional perfect, equivalent to 'would have traveled'.

examples.original: كَانَتْ سَتَقُولُ لَنَا الحَقِيقَةَ.
examples.phonetic: kānat sataqūlu lanā l-ḥaqīqata.
examples.translation: She was going to tell us the truth.
examples.note: Gender agreement: كَانَتْ for feminine, and the verb سَتَقُولُ also in feminine form.

levels.label: المستقبل في الماضي مع أَنْ
levels.translation: Future in the past with أَنْ (an)

examples.original: أَرَادَ أَنْ يَذْهَبَ إِلَى إِسْبَانِيَا.
examples.phonetic: ʔarāda ʔan yadhhaba ʔilā ʔisbāniyā.
examples.translation: He wanted to go to Spain.
examples.note: When using أَنْ + subjunctive verb, the future intention is inferred from context, but no explicit future marker is used.

examples.original: قَرَّرْنَا أَنْ نُسَافِرَ غَدًا.
examples.phonetic: qarrarnā ʔan nusāfira ɣadan.
examples.translation: We decided to travel tomorrow.
examples.note: Here, 'tomorrow' (غَدًا) is the temporal marker, though the verb is in the subjunctive.

examples.original: كَانَ يَأْمُلُ أَنْ يَتَعَلَّمَ العَرَبِيَّةَ.
examples.phonetic: kāna yaʔmulu ʔan yataʕallama l-ʕarabiyyata.
examples.translation: He hoped to learn Arabic.
examples.note: In this case, the expectation is future from the past, and the subjunctive with أَنْ is mandatory after verbs of desire or hope.

levels.label: المستقبل في الماضي مع سَوْفَ
levels.translation: Future in the past with سَوْفَ (sawfa)

examples.original: أَخْبَرَنِي أَنَّهُ سَوْفَ يَعُودُ بَعْدَ أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.phonetic: ʔaxbaranī ʔannahu sawfa yaʕūdu baʕda ʔusbūʕin.
examples.translation: He informed me that he would return after a week.
examples.note: سَوْفَ is used in indirect speech to mark a more distant or emphatic future.

examples.original: ظَنَنْتُ أَنَّهُمْ سَوْفَ يُوَافِقُونَ عَلَى الخُطَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: ẓanantu ʔannahum sawfa yuwāfiqūna ʕalā l-ḵuṭṭati.
examples.translation: I thought they would agree to the plan.
examples.note: Observe the masculine plural agreement in يُوَافِقُونَ.

examples.original: كَانَ مِنَ الوَاضِحِ أَنَّ المَشْرُوعَ سَوْفَ يَفْشَلُ.
examples.phonetic: kāna mina l-wāḍiḥi ʔanna l-mašrūʕa sawfa yafšalu.
examples.translation: It was clear that the project would fail.
examples.note: Here, سَوْفَ conveys a sense of certainty or inevitability, like 'was going to fail'.

translations.en: Complex Personal Narratives with Future Perspective

title: التقنيات المتقدمة في النقاش والرد / Advanced debate and refutation techniques
bridge: In Spanish, refutation often relies on explicit connectors like 'sin embargo' or 'no obstante', whereas Classical and dialectal Arabic employs syntactic structures such as emphatic negation with 'لا' and the use of particles like 'بل' to correct and contradict. Mastering these tools will allow you to nuance your arguments with precision. Pay attention to agreement in gender and number in nominal phrases when introducing counterarguments, a common error for Spanish speakers.
rule: To debate at a C1 level in Arabic, several resources are used: 1) The particle 'بل' (bal) to correct a previous statement: 'بل على العكس' (bal ʿalā al-ʿaks, 'on the contrary'). 2) The structure 'ما... بل...' (mā... bal...) to negate and affirm simultaneously: 'ما هذا صحيحًا بل هو خطأ' (mā hāḏā ṣaḥīḥan bal huwa ḫaṭaʾ). 3) The use of 'إنما' (innamā) to restrict: 'إنما المشكلة في التطبيق' (innamā al-muškilah fī al-taṭbīq). 4) The particle 'لو' (law) for hypothetical counterarguments: 'لو كان الأمر كذلك، لما فشلنا' (law kāna al-amr kaḏālika, lamā fašalnā). 5) Concessive expressions 'مع أن' (maʿa anna) and 'رغم أن' (raġma anna) followed by a noun or nominal phrase. Remember that in Arabic, the verb usually comes first, and negative modifiers like 'لم' (lam) and 'لن' (lan) require the apocopated form of the verb. In dialects, some particles are simplified (e.g., 'بس' instead of 'بل'), but for formal debate, Standard Arabic is preferred.

concept_examples.text: بل على العكس، هذا يعزز الموقف.
concept_examples.translation: On the contrary, this reinforces the position.
concept_examples.phonetic: bal ʿalā al-ʿaks, hāḏā yuʿazziz al-mawqif.

concept_examples.text: ما هذا صحيحًا بل هو مغالطة منطقية.
concept_examples.translation: This is not correct; rather, it is a logical fallacy.
concept_examples.phonetic: mā hāḏā ṣaḥīḥan bal huwa muġālaṭah manṭiqiyyah.

concept_examples.text: إنما الفرق الجوهري يكمن في السياق.
concept_examples.translation: The essential difference lies in the context.
concept_examples.phonetic: innamā al-farq al-ǧawharī yakmun fī al-siyāq.

concept_examples.text: لو سلمنا بفرضيتك، فلا يلزم أن تكون النتيجة حتمية.
concept_examples.translation: If we accept your hypothesis, it does not necessarily follow that the outcome is inevitable.
concept_examples.phonetic: law sallamnā bifarḍiyyatika, falā yalzam an takūn al-natīǧah ḥatmiyyah.

common_error.wrong: لا أوافق لأن رأيك ضعيف، ولكن أنا أرى أن...
common_error.correct: لا أوافق لأن حجتك ضعيفة، بل أرى أن...
common_error.correct_alt: لا أوافق على ذلك، إذ إن حجتك ضعيفة، بل أرى أن...
common_error.explanation: A common mistake is overusing 'ولكن' (but), translating directly from Spanish, when in Arabic 'بل' (rather) is more forceful for refutation. Additionally, 'رأيك' (your opinion) is too personal; in formal debate, 'حجتك' (your argument) is preferred to maintain objectivity. Explicit use of 'أنت' should also be avoided in formal contexts, as Arabic favors impersonal phrasing.

examples.original: لا أوافق على هذا الطرح، بل أعتبره غير دقيق.
examples.phonetic: lā uwāfiq ʿalā hāḏā al-ṭarḥ, bal aʿtabiruhu ġayr daqīq.
examples.translation: I do not agree with this proposal; rather, I consider it imprecise.
examples.note: Use of 'لا' + present verb, followed by 'بل' to correct.

examples.original: على النقيض من ذلك، الأدلة تشير إلى عكس ما تزعم.
examples.phonetic: ʿalā al-naqīḍ min ḏālika, al-adillah tušīr ilā ʿaks mā tazʿum.
examples.translation: On the contrary, the evidence points to the opposite of what you claim.
examples.note: Expression 'على النقيض من ذلك' is useful for introducing opposition.

examples.original: قد يكون هذا صحيحًا في بعض الحالات، لكنه ليس قاعدة عامة.
examples.phonetic: qad yakūn hāḏā ṣaḥīḥan fī baʿḍ al-ḥālāt, lākinnahu laysa qāʿidah ʿāmmah.
examples.translation: This may be true in some cases, but it is not a general rule.
examples.note: Partial concession with 'قد' and 'لكن' to soften the statement.

examples.original: إذا افترضنا صحة مبدئك، فستكون النتائج متناقضة.
examples.phonetic: iḏā f-taraḍnā ṣiḥḥat mabdaʾika, fasatakūn al-natāʾiǧ mutanāqiḍah.
examples.translation: If we assume the validity of your principle, the results will be contradictory.
examples.note: Conditional 'إذا' followed by a past verb to indicate a supposition.

examples.original: لو أنك راجعت المصادر، لأدركت خطأ استنتاجك.
examples.phonetic: law annaka rāǧaʿta al-maṣādir, laʾadrakt ḫaṭaʾ istintāǧik.
examples.translation: If you had reviewed the sources, you would have noticed the error in your conclusion.
examples.note: Counterfactual conditional with 'لو' + response with 'لاما'.

examples.original: لا يلزم من صحة المقدمة صحة النتيجة.
examples.phonetic: lā yalzam min ṣiḥḥat al-muqaddimah ṣiḥḥat al-natīǧah.
examples.translation: The validity of the premise does not necessarily imply the validity of the conclusion.
examples.note: General negation with 'لا يلزم' to indicate lack of logical necessity.

examples.original: أرى أن حجتك تفتقر إلى الدقة، لأنك تجاهلت العوامل الاقتصادية.
examples.phonetic: arā anna ḥuǧǧataka taftaqir ilā al-diqqah, liʾannaka taǧāhalt al-ʿawāmil al-iqtiṣādiyyah.
examples.translation: I see that your argument lacks precision because you ignored economic factors.
examples.note: Use of 'أرى أن' to soften criticism.

examples.original: بدلًا من التعميم، ينبغي أن تميز بين الحالات المختلفة.
examples.phonetic: badalan min al-taʿmīm, yanbaġī an tumayyiz bayn al-ḥālāt al-muḫtalifah.
examples.translation: Instead of generalizing, you should distinguish between different cases.
examples.note: Expression 'بدلًا من' to propose an alternative.

examples.original: من الممكن أن نتفق على المبادئ، لكن نختلف في التطبيق.
examples.phonetic: min al-mumkin an nattafiq ʿalā al-mabādiʾ, lākin naḫtalif fī al-taṭbīq.
examples.translation: We may agree on the principles, but we differ in their application.
examples.note: Softening with 'من الممكن' and contrast with 'لكن'.

title: المصطلحات الأكاديمية المتخصصة / Academic specialized vocabulary
bridge: In Spanish, academic vocabulary is often formed with Latin and Greek roots and adapts easily (e.g., 'hipótesis', 'metodología'). In Arabic, however, academic vocabulary is built from triliteral roots with internal vowel patterns that change meaning (e.g., 'نَظَرَ' (to look) → 'نَظَرِيَّة' (theory)). Modern Standard Arabic (fus·ḥā) also uses complex syntactic structures like 'إضافة' (construct state) and relative clauses that have no direct equivalent in Spanish. A common trap for Spanish speakers is to translate academic adjectives ending in -ico/-al literally, when Arabic prefers abstract nouns or nominal structures (e.g., 'الطريقة العلمية' instead of 'الطريقة العلمي').
rule: In C1 Arabic, specialized academic vocabulary is characterized by: 1) Derivation through patterns: most terms are derived from triliteral roots with schemas such as 'فَعْل' (action noun), 'فِعَال' (process noun), 'مَفْعَل' (place/time), 'فَعَّال' (intensive adjective), 'إفْعَال' (causative). For example, 'بحث' (search/investigation) from the root ب-ح-ث, 'مبحث' (research topic), 'باحِث' (researcher), 'أبحاث' (investigations, irregular plural). 2) Construct state (إضافة): very productive in academic Arabic, used to express possession or specification, such as 'منهجية البحث' (research methodology). 3) Case system: Classical Arabic declines nominative, genitive, and accusative cases; in academic register, correct use of vocalic endings is expected, though in spoken Modern Standard Arabic they are often omitted. 4) Prefixes and suffixes: prefixes like 'لا-' (non-) and 'ما-' (negation vowel) are used in terms like 'لاوعي' (unconscious) and 'ماوراء' (metaphysical). 5) Broken plurals: very frequent in technical vocabulary (e.g., 'نظريات' from 'نظرية', 'مفاهيم' from 'مفهوم'). 6) Prepositional phrases and locutions: prepositions such as 'في' (in), 'من' (of), 'إلى' (to), 'على' (on) are used to nuance logical relations (e.g., 'استنادًا إلى' (based on), 'بخصوص' (regarding)). 7) Use of 'أنّ' and 'أنَّ' for nominal clauses and causatives: 'يُعتقد أنّ' (it is believed that). At C1 level, students are expected to distinguish between academic (scientific) Arabic and colloquial Arabic, avoid anglicized constructions, and use formulas typical of Arabic academic writing, such as introductions, theses, and author references.

concept_examples.text: يَمثُلُ المَفهومُ الأساسيُّ في هذه الدراسةِ إلى تَحليلِ البِنى المَعْرِفِيَّةِ في نَظريَّاتِ التعليمِ.
concept_examples.translation: The fundamental concept of this study lies in the analysis of cognitive structures in educational theories.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈjamθulu l-mafˈhuːmu l-ʔaˈsaːsijju fiː haːðihi d-diˈraːsati ʔilaː taħˈliːli l-binaː l-maʕrifijjati fiː naðaˈrijjaːti t-taʕˈliːm

concept_examples.text: تَتَعَدَّدُ المَنهجِيَّاتُ المتبَّعةُ في الدِّراساتِ اللِّسانيَّةِ؛ مِنها الوَصفيَّةُ والتَّوليديَّةُ والنَّقديَّةُ.
concept_examples.translation: The methodologies employed in linguistic studies are multiple; among them, the descriptive, generative, and critical ones.
concept_examples.phonetic: taˈtaʕaddad al-munhaˈdʒijjaːt al-mutˈtabaʕa fiː d-diraːˈsaːt al-lisaːˈnijjaːt; ˈminhaː al-wasˈfijja wal-tawˈliːdijja wan-naqˈdijja

concept_examples.text: يَستَنِدُ تَحقيقُ الهويَّةِ اللُّغويَّةِ إلى الإطارِ التَّاريخيِّ والثَّقافيِّ في الوطَنِ العَرَبيِّ.
concept_examples.translation: The realization of linguistic identity is grounded in the historical and cultural framework of the Arab world.
concept_examples.phonetic: jasˈtanidu taħˈqiːqu l-hawijjati l-luɣaˈwijja ʔilaː l-ʔiˈtˤaːr at-taːriːxiː waθ-θaqaːfiː fiː l-watˤan al-ʕarabij

concept_examples.text: تُشكِّلُ النُّصوصُ البَلاغيَّةُ وتَحليلُ خِطابِها مِحورًا مِنهاجيًّا في الدِّراساتِ الأَكاديمِيَّةِ المُعاصِرَةِ.
concept_examples.translation: Rhetorical texts and their discourse analysis constitute a methodological core in contemporary academic studies.
concept_examples.phonetic: tuˈʃakkilu n-nusuːs al-balaːɣijja wa-taħˈliːlu xiˈtˤaːbihaː mihˈwaran minhaːdʒiijan fiː d-diraːsaːt al-ʔakˌaːdiːˈmijja al-muˈʕaːsjra

common_error.wrong: المَنْهَج العِلْمِي يَتَكَفَّل بَتَحقيقِ الأهدافِ البَحْثِيَّة
common_error.correct: المَنْهَجُ العِلْمِيُّ يَتَكَفَّلُ بِتَحقيقِ الأهدافِ البَحثيَّةِ
common_error.correct_alt: يَتَكَفَّلُ المَنْهَجُ العِلْمِيُّ بِتَحقيقِ الأهدافِ البَحثيَّةِ
common_error.explanation: The main error is omitting the correct case ending (المَنْهَجُ in nominative, and proper declension of 'الأهدافِ' in genitive after the preposition 'بِـ'). Spanish speakers, unaccustomed to case systems, often forget the correct final vocalization; word order (subject+verb) is grammatically correct, but the typical Arabic word order is verb-subject (VSO), though SVO is also accepted in Modern Standard Arabic. However, in academic contexts, VSO is preferred. Care should be taken with number and gender agreement, and the use of the definite article (الـ) with nouns and adjectives.

examples.original: الفَرَضِيَّةُ الرَّئيسِيَّةُ تَعْتَمِدُ على مُعْطَياتٍ إحْصائِيَّةٍ مُعَقَّدَةٍ.
examples.phonetic: al-faˈradˤijja ur-raʔiːsijja taʕˈtamidu ʕalaː muʕˈtˤajˈjaːt ʔiħˈsˤaːʔijja muˈʕaqqada
examples.translation: The main hypothesis relies on complex statistical data.
examples.note: The word 'الفرضية' (hypothesis) is derived from 'فرض' (to assume) and the adjective 'الرئيسية' (main) in a construct state (idāfa) structure.

examples.original: لِتَحْقيقِ المَصداقِيَّةِ في البَحْثِ، نَعْتَمِدُ على التَّثْبُّتِ مِنَ الأَدَواتِ البَحْثيَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: li-taħˈqiːqi l-misˈdaːqijja fiː l-baħθi natˈtamidu ʕalaː t-tabˈbuti mina l-ʔadaˈwaːt al-baħθijja
examples.translation: To achieve credibility in research, we rely on the verification of research tools.
examples.note: Use of 'لـ' (in order to), 'مصداقية' (credibility) and 'أدوات' (tools, broken plural).

examples.original: يَتَطَلَّبُ المَنْهَجُ الوَصْفِيُّ جَمْعَ عَيِّنَةٍ تَمْثيلِيَّةٍ مِنَ المُجْتَمَعِ المُسْتَهْدَفِ.
examples.phonetic: jataˈtˤallabu l-manhadʒu l-wasfijju dʒamʕa ʕajjina tamˈθiːlijja mina l-mudʒtamaʕi l-mustahˈdaf
examples.translation: The descriptive method requires collecting a representative sample from the target population.
examples.note: Emphasis on 'يَتَطَلَّبُ' (requires) and the use of 'مِن' + genitive to complete the prepositional phrase.

examples.original: تَتَبايَنُ الدَّلالاتُ النَّحْوِيَّةُ في الجُمَلِ الشَّرْطِيَّةِ بَيْنَ اللُّغَتَيْنِ العَرَبِيَّةِ والإِسْبانِيَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: tatabaːjanu ad-dalaːˈlaːt un-naħˈwijja fiː l-dʒumal aʃ-ʃarˈtˤijja bajna l-luɣatajn al-ʕarabijja wa-l-ʔisbaːnijja
examples.translation: Syntactic meanings in conditional sentences differ between Arabic and Spanish.
examples.note: Use of 'تَتَبايَنُ' (differ) and 'دلالات' (meanings/semantics) in broken plural form.

examples.original: يُعَدُّ تَحليلُ الخِطابِ أَداةً تَفْسيرِيَّةً لِكَشْفِ الإِبْهامِ في النُّصوصِ الأَكاديمِيَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: juʕaddu taħˈliːlu l-xitˤaːbi ʔadaːtan tafsirijja li-kashfi l-ʔibhaːmi fiː n-nusuːs al-ʔakˈaːdimiːjja
examples.translation: Discourse analysis is an interpretive tool for revealing ambiguity in academic texts.
examples.note: The structure 'يُعَدُّ' (is considered) and the use of 'كَشْفِ' (revealing) in construct state.

examples.original: تَتَضَمَّنُ البَلاغَةُ العَرَبِيَّةُ مَفاهيمَ مِثلَ التَّوازي والتَّضادِّ في بِناءِ الحُجَّةِ.
examples.phonetic: tataˈdammadu l-balaːɣa al-ʕarabijja mafaˈhiːma miθla t-tawaːziː wat-taˈdˤaːd fiː biˈnaːʔ il-ħudʒa
examples.translation: Arabic rhetoric includes concepts such as parallelism and antithesis in argument construction.
examples.note: Use of 'تَتَضَمَّنُ' (includes) and 'مفاهيم' (concepts) as a broken plural of 'مفهوم'.

levels.label: الإِطاراتُ النَّظَرِيَّةُ والمَدارِسُ الفِكْرِيَّةُ
levels.translation: Theoretical frameworks and schools of thought

examples.original: أَثَّرَتِ المَدرَسَةُ البِنْيَوِيَّةُ في الدِّراساتِ اللِّسانيَّةِ الحَديثَةِ تَأثيرًا تَأسيسِيًّا.
examples.phonetic: ʔaθθarat al-madrasa al-binjawijja fiː d-diraːsaːt al-lisaːnijja al-ħadiːθa taʔˈsiːran taʔˈsiːsijjan
examples.translation: Structuralism influenced modern linguistic studies in a foundational way.
examples.note: Use of 'مدرسة' (school), 'بنيوية' (structuralist) and the accusative internal object (تأثيرًا).

examples.original: يُوازِنُ الباحِثونَ بَيْنَ النَّماذَجِ السَّلَفِيَّةِ والتَّكْوينيَّةِ في تَأصيلِ المَفهومِ التَّاريخِيّ.
examples.phonetic: juwaːzinu l-baːħiθuːna bajna n-namaːdʒi s-salaˈfijja wat-takwiːnijja fiː taʔˈsiːli l-mafhuum at-tariːxiː
examples.translation: Researchers balance between classical and constructivist models in grounding the historical concept.
examples.note: Use of 'يُوازِنُ' (to balance) and 'نماذج' (models) as an irregular plural.

examples.original: تَتَجاوَبُ النِّظريَّةُ النَّقْدِيَّةُ مَعَ الإِشْكاليَّاتِ المَعْرِفِيَّةِ المُعاصِرَةِ مُتَّخِذَةً مَوقِعًا تَحْليليًّا.
examples.phonetic: tataʔdʒaːwabu n-naðarijja naqˈdijja maʕa l-ʔiʃkaːlijjaːt al-maʕrifijja muʕaːsjra mutaxiðan mawqiʕan taħliːlijan
examples.translation: Critical theory engages with contemporary epistemological issues by adopting an analytical stance.
examples.note: Use of 'تَتَجاوَبُ' (to engage) and 'مُتَّخِذَةً' (adopting) in active accusative form.

title: التعبيرات الاصطلاحية واللغة العامية / Idiomatic expressions and colloquial language
bridge: In Arabic, we use expressions like 'على قلب واحد' (literally 'in one heart') to mean 'in agreement,' similar to Spanish idioms such as 'estar en las nubes' or 'tirar la toalla.' However, their structure and imagery can differ greatly. A common mistake is translating these expressions literally from Spanish, which results in unnatural or even humorous phrases. To master them, you must learn them as whole units, paying attention to their register (formal vs. colloquial) and the contexts in which they are used.
rule: Arabic idiomatic expressions and colloquial language are characterized by: 1) Frequent use of metaphors rooted in Arab culture (e.g., 'على قلب واحد' for 'in agreement'). 2) Many expressions are built with verbs like 'أكل' (to eat), 'شرب' (to drink), or 'مشى' (to walk), which are often unpredictable. 3) Colloquial registers vary by region (Egypt, the Levant, the Gulf, etc.), though some expressions are common across the Arab world, especially in Modern Standard Arabic. 4) Context is key: some expressions are informal and should not be used in formal settings. 5) Many expressions have a fixed structure and do not allow word order changes. 6) Intonation and body language are crucial for understanding tone (humor, sarcasm, etc.). At the C1 level, learners should recognize and use these expressions naturally, adapting them to the appropriate register.

concept_examples.text: هذا الموضوع مش على بعضه.
concept_examples.translation: This matter is not coherent / This topic doesn’t make sense.
concept_examples.phonetic: haːðaː al-mawduːʕ muʃ ʕalaː baʕdˤih

concept_examples.text: ضربت على وتر حساس.
concept_examples.translation: You touched a raw nerve.
concept_examples.phonetic: dˤarabat ʕalaː watar ħassaːs

concept_examples.text: يُوكل للحكي ما يخلص.
concept_examples.translation: He never stops talking (a never-ending talker).
concept_examples.phonetic: juːkal lil-ħakiː maː jixallasˤ

concept_examples.text: على قد حاله.
concept_examples.translation: He is very humble / of modest means.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʕalaː qadd ħaluh

common_error.explanation: This error comes from translating the Spanish idiom 'estar en las nubes' (to be daydreaming) literally. In Arabic, the imagery of 'clouds' is used differently; a natural equivalent might be 'lost in the air' (طايش في الهوا) or 'lost in the clouds' (تايِه في السحاب), but 'في الغيوم' is not idiomatic in this figurative sense. To avoid such mistakes, learn expressions as whole units without word-for-word translation, and pay attention to Arabic-specific constructions.

examples.original: رايح في ستين داهية.
examples.phonetic: raːjiħ fiː settiːn daːhiya
examples.translation: Going through sixty disasters (describes someone who is lost or in trouble).
examples.note: This expression uses the number 'sixty' as an exaggeration, common in Arabic. It is hyperbolic, not literal.

examples.original: ولّع في قلبي نار.
examples.phonetic: walliʕ fiː qalbi naːr
examples.translation: You lit a fire in my heart (it moved me deeply or made me very angry).
examples.note: Fire symbolizes strong emotions. Compare with Spanish 'prender fuego,' but here it is emotional.

examples.original: سمعت كل كلمة على أذني.
examples.phonetic: samiʕt kull kalima ʕalaː ʔuðni
examples.translation: I heard every word with my ears (i.e., attentively).
examples.note: In Arabic, the preposition 'on' (على) is used instead of 'with.' It is a fixed construction.

examples.original: على راسي.
examples.phonetic: ʕalaː raːsi
examples.translation: It’s an honor (literally 'on my head,' used as a response to a request).
examples.note: A very common expression in service contexts. It does not mean 'in my head' but 'I’ll do it gladly.'

examples.original: خلّيها على الله.
examples.phonetic: xalliːha ʕalaː allaːh
examples.translation: Leave it to God (i.e., I can’t do anything about it, or don’t worry).
examples.note: Reflects the Islamic culture of entrusting outcomes to God. It is a form of consolation.

examples.original: ما في شي ببلاش.
examples.phonetic: maː fiː ʃiː b-balaːʃ
examples.translation: Nothing is free.
examples.note: Levantine colloquialism using 'ببلاش' (for free). A fatalistic common expression.

examples.original: بدك تلحس وِجّك.
examples.phonetic: bidak tilħas wijjak
examples.translation: You’ll regret it (literally 'you’ll lick your face').
examples.note: A colloquial threat or warning, very graphic and informal.

examples.original: هذا إنسان مية بالمية.
examples.phonetic: haːðaː ʔinsaːn miyya bil-miyya
examples.translation: This person is one hundred percent (reliable, complete).
examples.note: Using 'percent' to emphasize quality. Can also describe 'قهوة مية بالمية' (pure coffee).

examples.original: شخص بلا روح.
examples.phonetic: ʃaxsˤ bilaː ruːħ
examples.translation: A person without a soul (boring or lacking energy).
examples.note: The soul (روح) symbolizes vitality. Compare with Spanish 'sin vida' (without life).

examples.original: عنده لسان طويل.
examples.phonetic: ʕandu lisaːn tˤawiːl
examples.translation: He has a long tongue (he’s a gossip or talks too much).
examples.note: In Spanish, we say 'tener mucha lengua' or 'ser un lenguaraz.' In Arabic, the image is based on length.

translations.en: Authentic use of colloquial language and idioms

title: التعابير الاصطلاحية والمجازية في السياقات المهنية والاجتماعية / Idiomatic and metaphorical expressions in professional and social contexts
bridge: In Arabic, idiomatic expressions often rely on bodily and cultural metaphors that do not have a direct equivalent in Spanish. For example, 'يده طويلة' (literally 'his hand is long') means to have influence or power, while in Spanish one would say 'tener mucha mano' or 'tener contactos'. Additionally, Arabic uses verbal and nominal structures that differ from Spanish, such as the construction 'ما أفعله' to express admiration, which does not exist in Spanish. A common mistake is to translate Spanish expressions literally, such as 'estar en las nubes', which in Arabic would be 'رأسه في السحاب' (his head in the clouds) but is not used; instead, one says 'عقله طاير' (his mind flying).
rule: In Arabic, idiomatic expressions are divided into three main categories: 1) Bodily expressions (using parts of the body like 'يد' (hand) or 'عين' (eye)): for example, 'عينه على' (his eye on) means 'to be interested in something'. 2) Expressions of movement and direction: such as 'ذهب إلى' (to go to) used metaphorically, for example 'ذهبت نفسه إلى' (his soul went to) means 'to long for'. 3) Cultural and religious expressions: such as 'إن شاء الله' (God willing) used to express hope or intention, but also as a courtesy to reject something without offending. To speak with near-native fluency, it is crucial to master the use of these expressions in appropriate contexts, paying attention to register (formal/informal) and dialect. In Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), fixed forms are used, while in dialects there are variations. For example, in MSA one says 'لا شك في ذلك' (there is no doubt about that), but in Egyptian dialect one says 'مفيش شك' (there is no doubt). Additionally, many idiomatic expressions are untranslatable and require knowledge of Arab culture to use them correctly.

concept_examples.text: يده طويلة في الشركة، يقدر يوصلك لأي منصب.
concept_examples.translation: His hand is long in the company, he can get you to any position.
concept_examples.phonetic: /jadu-hu tˤawiːla fi‿ʃ-ʃarika, jaqdir juwasˤsˤilak li-ʔayyi mansˤib/

concept_examples.text: عقله طاير من كتر الشغل.
concept_examples.translation: His mind is flying from so much work.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʕaqlu tˤaːir min kuthr aʃ-ʃuɣl/

concept_examples.text: قلبه أبيض، ما بيغشش حد.
concept_examples.translation: His heart is white, he doesn’t deceive anyone.
concept_examples.phonetic: /qalbu ʔabjadˤ, ma bijɣaʃʃiʃ ħad/

concept_examples.text: ما تزعلش، دي الدنيا وما فيها.
concept_examples.translation: Don’t get upset, that’s life and what’s in it.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ma tizʕalʃ, di‿d-dunja wa ma fiːha/

common_error.wrong: أنا في السحاب (literal translation of 'estoy en las nubes')
common_error.explanation: The mistake occurs because the student translates the Spanish expression 'estar en las nubes' literally into Arabic. In Arabic, this image does not exist; instead, one uses a metaphor of a flying mind ('عقله طاير') or directly expresses lack of concentration. To avoid this, it is important to learn Arabic idiomatic expressions as complete units, not word-for-word translations. It is also useful to practice with native speakers and pay attention to the expressions they use in real contexts.

examples.original: يده خفيفة في الشغل
examples.phonetic: /jadu xuˈfiːfa fi‿ʃ-ʃuɣl/
examples.translation: His hand is light at work (he’s skillful)
examples.note: This expression is used to describe someone who is skillful and quick at their job. The metaphor of the 'light hand' is specific to Arabic; in Spanish one might say 'es un manitas' or 'tiene buena mano'.

examples.original: عينه على المنصب
examples.phonetic: /ʕajnu ʕala‿l-manṣib/
examples.translation: His eye is on the position (he’s interested in the position)
examples.note: Used to express interest or desire for something. In Spanish, one might say 'tiene el ojo puesto en algo', but in Arabic it is more common with 'عين'.

examples.original: رجله على قلبه
examples.phonetic: /riʒlu ʕala qalbu/
examples.translation: His foot is on his heart (he’s calm, at peace)
examples.note: An idiomatic expression indicating tranquility or satisfaction. It is a metaphorical image that does not exist in Spanish, so it must be memorized.

examples.original: مشيت على طول
examples.phonetic: /miʃit ʕala tˤuːl/
examples.translation: I walked straight (I went straight to the point)
examples.note: In conversational context, this phrase is used to indicate that someone was direct or without beating around the bush. It is an idiomatic expression that uses movement to refer to communication.

examples.original: دخل في الموضوع على طول
examples.phonetic: /daxal fi‿l-mawdˤuʕ ʕala tˤuːl/
examples.translation: He went straight into the topic (he got to the point)
examples.note: Similar to the previous one, used to describe someone who addresses a topic without hesitation. In Spanish one would say 'fue directo al asunto'.

examples.original: طلع من الموضوع
examples.phonetic: /tˤalaʕ min al-mawdˤuʕ/
examples.translation: He left the topic (he digressed)
examples.note: Used when someone changes the subject or gets sidetracked. It is a spatial metaphor: leaving a place (the topic).

examples.original: يعطيك العافية
examples.phonetic: /jaʕtˤiːk al-ʕaːfija/
examples.translation: May He give you health (thanks, recognition)
examples.note: A very common expression in Arab countries to thank or recognize effort. Used in formal and informal contexts. It has no direct equivalent in Spanish.

examples.original: الله يسلمك
examples.phonetic: /allaːh jisallimak/
examples.translation: May God protect you (polite response to thanks)
examples.note: Used as a response to 'شكرًا' (thank you) or a compliment. Equivalent to 'de nada' but with a religious nuance. At C1 level, it is important to know when to use it.

examples.original: بصراحة، الموضوع صعب
examples.phonetic: /bisˤraːħa, al-mawdˤuʕ sˤaʕb/
examples.translation: Frankly, the topic is difficult
examples.note: The use of 'بصراحة' (with honesty) is common to soften negative opinions. In Spanish, one might say 'siendo honesto' or 'francamente'.
